A_target.statement:
Let $\GF q$ be a [[Definition:Finite Field|finite field]].
Then [[Definition:Vector Space|vector spaces]] over $\GF q$ have [[Definition:Basis (Linear Algebra)|bases]], a well-defined [[Definition:Dimension of Vector Space|dimension]], the [[Rank-Nullity Theorem]] and [[Definition:Determinant of Matrix|determinants]], but no order or [[Definition:Inner Product|inner product]] geometry.

B_source.statement: [[Definition:Vector Space|Vector spaces]] over $\R$ have [[Definition:Basis (Linear Algebra)|bases]], [[Definition:Dimension of Vector Space|dimension]], the [[Rank-Nullity Theorem]], and [[Definition:Orthogonal (Linear Algebra)|orthogonality]] with respect to [[Definition:Inner Product|inner products]].

substitutions.the real vector space: a vector space over the finite field
substitutions.row reduction over the reals: row reduction over the finite field

derived.bases, dimension and rank-nullity: unchanged, since their proofs use only the field axioms
derived.orthogonality and positive definiteness: lost, since no ordering or positivity is available

validity_conditions: The proofs of basis existence, well-definedness of dimension, and rank-nullity use only the field axioms, so they transfer verbatim.
Inner product geometry does not transfer: without an ordering there is no positivity, and a nonzero vector can be orthogonal to itself under the standard bilinear form.
In characteristic p the trace of the identity vanishes when p divides the dimension, so trace arguments that assume it is nonzero fail and must be avoided.
proof_plan:
Replace $\R$ by $\GF q$.
The proofs of the basic results use only the [[Definition:Field Axioms|field axioms]].
Existence of bases, [[Invariance of Dimension of Vector Space|invariance of dimension]] and the [[Rank-Nullity Theorem]] transfer unchanged.

Results relying on ordering or positivity, such as $\innerprod v v > 0$ for $v \ne 0$, [[Definition:Positive Definite Matrix|positive definiteness]] and the [[Spectral Theorem]], are discarded.
For example, in $\GF 2^2$ the vector $\tuple {1, 1}$ satisfies $\tuple {1, 1} \cdot \tuple {1, 1} = 0$.
